newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Two Cyprus sides ready for U.N. talks, but wary.
newsitem.headline: Two Cyprus sides ready for U.N. talks, but wary.

text.p: Greeks and Turks on the divided island of Cyprus on Friday reaffirmed they were ready to start settlement talks in July at the urging of the United Nations, but appeared wary of the intentions of their negotiating partners.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has tentatively set a July 9 date to convene face-to-face talks between the two leaders, his spokesman said on Thursday.
The talks would be the first known encounter in nearly three years between Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides, head of the Greek Cypriot community, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Peace efforts on the island suffered a serious setback last year after a series of killings along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone separating the two communities. Tensions also ran high in January after disclosure that the Greek Cypriots had ordered air-defence missiles from Russia.
Turkey, which maintains 30,000 troops in northern Cyprus, vowed to block missile deployment.
The announcement of face-to-face talks capped months of preparatory talks by U.N. envoys.

But it caused little excitement among Cypriots, whose country has been divided since a Turkish invasion in 1974 after a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Since then the U.N. has failed to broker reunification under a federal system.
Denktash, who heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north, recognised only by Turkey, on Friday said his side was open to talks.

"But the purpose of talks cannot be making the Greek Cypriots the legitimate government, watering down the guarantee agreements, replacing the Turkish guarantee rights by a multinational force and tying the Turkish Cypriots to Greece in the name of European Union membership," he said, referring to the long-standing Turkish position that Cyprus cannot be a member state of an organisation which does not include both Greece or Turkey.
Denktash said: "It is worth talking to Clerides for a couple of days to tell him that. Thinking that you can solve the Cyprus problem with missiles does not befit a clever leader."
Greece is a member of the European Union. Turkey formally applied to join in 1987.
Manolis Christofides, spokesman of the Greek-Cypriot government, said the Greek Cypriots would go to the talks to cooperate sincerely with a spirit of goodwill.
He said the government has assurances that officials from the U.S., Britain, the U.N. and Europe will be on the sidelines of the meeting and have pledged to offer their assistance.

He said the Greek Cypriots were putting aside pessimism born from the lack of progress noted during proximity talks held over the past three months by the United Nations. The talks were preparatory ones to the direct summit.
"The dynamism of these key players may result in a breakthrough, even a breakthrough on Turkish intransigence," he said.

Diplomats said that with Cyprus about to start accession talks with the European Union next year, the killings last summer and closer international focus on the dispute were bound to spur movement and yield some positive results at the forthcoming summit.
"The secretary-general wouldn't have decided to call the talks unless there is serious prospect for movement this time," said a European diplomat in Nicosia.
